title: Abstract,Australia’s East Coast Gas Market (ECGM) is widely regarded as a policy paradox. Despite abundant gas reserves, households, businesses and industry continue to face high energy costs. While these outcomes are often tied to the ECGM’s integration with the global gas and oil markets, such explanations do not account for the narrow scope of regulatory reform and the political constraints shaping domestic energy policy. This article examines how export-oriented gas markets shape domestic energy governance and constrain political feasibility of sustained regulatory intervention to safeguard domestic users. It focuses on three recurring claims that dominate political debate - increasing gas supply lowers prices, renewable energy is unreliable, and that governments can regulate the industry effectively - and how these claims stabilise regulatory limits despite evidence of market inefficacies and rising domestic energy costs.
